extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, students of drama, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging Tragedy (and related poetic genres) according to Aristotelian poetics: how plot, character, language, metre, and spectacle should be organized and why. Intended to guide poets/playwrights and critics in producing or assessing dramatic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (Imitation) as the basis of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is fundamentally an imitation (mimesis) of actions, persons, and life; humans take pleasure in likenesses because in contemplating them they are engaged in learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure from imitation arises from the exercise of inference and recognition ('this is the man'); if the original is unseen, pleasure may be due to execution (coloring, craft) rather than imitation per se. The poet imitates actions, not merely people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct for harmony and rhythm (metre)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural human instinct for harmony and rhythm; metre is a species of rhythm and a fundamental element of poetic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons with this natural gift refined early improvisations into poetry. Choice of metre must suit the subject (see separate criteria on metre suitability). Rhythm and metre are intrinsic to poetic form and affect audience receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching of poetry by poet's character (genre by bent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry branched into types according to individual character: elevated poets imitated noble actions; more trivial poets imitated meaner persons (satire/comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'natural bent' of writers led them to compose either Comedy (ludicrous/meaner actions) or Tragedy/Epic (noble actions). Example: Homer preeminent among serious poets and influential for subsequent dramatic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter suitability to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain metres are more fitting to particular subjects: e.g., iambic metre suits lampooning/lampooning measure, hexameter for epic, trochaic tetrameter for satyric/dancing affinities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The iambic is colloquial and matches conversational speech; hexameters are narrative and less colloquial. Choice of metre thus affects tone and appropriateness for comedy, tragedy, or epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in embellished language (rhythm, harmony, song); in dramatic form (not narrative); effecting through pity and fear the proper purgation (catharsis) of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embellished language includes rhythm, harmony and melody; parts of a tragedy may be rendered through verse alone or with song. The imitation is of action (praxis), not merely of character or narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language embellished (rhythm, harmony, song) as quality criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of tragic language depends on inclusion of rhythm, harmony, and song—different kinds of artistic ornament appearing in separate parts of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some parts are rendered through verse only, others with song; the presence and apt use of these ornaments is a mark of artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the chief element (the soul of tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot (mythos) — the arrangement of incidents — is the first principle and soul of tragedy; it determines the work's quality and is the principal object of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must be a complete whole (beginning, middle, end), of appropriate magnitude, and unity: the parts must be causally connected so that displacement/removal of any part disjoins the whole. Plotting should aim at probability or necessity, not mere chronology or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos) as subsidiary to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that which reveals moral purpose (what a person chooses or avoids) and ranks second to plot; characters supply the agents through whom actions occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character must be consistent and appropriate to the actions, but action is primary: there can be tragedy without finely drawn character, but not without action. Dialogue should indicate choice and volition to express character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) — reasoning and the expression of general truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of stating what is possible and pertinent—proving, asserting general maxims, and the intellectual content behind speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dialogue, this is the function of political/rhetorical art (older poets use civic speech, later poets rhetorical language). Thought contributes to the persuasive and philosophical dimension of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (Lexis) — the expression of meaning in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the metrical arrangement and choice of words; it is the expression of meaning and is essentially the same in verse or prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction includes naming and interpretation and carries power both in metrical and non-metrical utterance; it should be well-chosen but ranks after plot, character, and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (Melopoeia) as central embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song (melody/melopoeia) is the chief of the embellishments and an important means of imitation and emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song is employed in some parts of a tragedy (e.g., choral parts) and contributes strongly to the aesthetic effect; it ranks among the five principal elements beyond the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle/Scenery (Opsis) — the least artistic element
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery (visual spectacle) has emotional attraction but is the least artistic and least connected with poetic theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenic effects depend more on the stage manager's art than the poet's; while powerful, spectacle is not the central criterion of poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis: effecting pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper tragedy through representation of action should arouse and then purge (catharsis) the emotions of pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This therapeutic/purificatory function is a core aim; construction of incidents (reversal, recognition) is calibrated to produce this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single, whole action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must imitate one action, a whole whose parts are so structured that if any part is displaced or removed the whole is disjointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of action is not unity of hero; one person's life contains many actions that cannot be made into a single dramatic action. The action must be causally coherent and self-contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness: beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic whole must have a beginning (which itself does not follow anything by necessity), a middle (which follows and is followed), and an end (which naturally follows something but has nothing following it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginnings and ends must not be arbitrary; the plot must conform to this causal/natural sequence so the whole reads as a complete unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Proper length
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must be of a certain magnitude: large enough to encompass a complete action and allow probable change (good→bad or bad→good), but not so long as to be incomprehensible in one view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper magnitude is such that the sequence of events can be embraced by memory and the audience; extremes (too short or excessively long) damage the aesthetic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity (plausibility over mere factuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should present what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity, not merely relate what has happened (that is the historian's task).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry aims at the universal (what typically would happen) while history records particulars. Plausibility (the possible) legitimizes invented plots and names—events need not be historical to be poetic if they are credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of epeisodic plots (episodic, disconnected incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots — where episodes/acts succeed without probable or necessary sequence — are the worst kind of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such episodic composition often stems from writers tailoring for performers or competitions; good plotting ensures causal/probable sequence rather than disjointed episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals of fortune (peripeteia) and recognitions (anagnorisis) are chief elements that produce powerful emotional interest in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novices often perfect diction or character before they can frame incidents; reversals and recognitions are plot mechanisms that heighten catharsis and should be employed artfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character must indicate moral purpose (proairesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character reveals a person's moral purpose — the sort of thing they choose or avoid — and must inform actions within the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If speech does not indicate what a speaker chooses or avoids, it fails to express character. Ethical portraiture should be consistent but serves the action rather than replacing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic unity (each part necessary to the whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly constructed tragic whole is organic: each part exists for the whole, and the removal or displacement of a proper part will disturb the integrity of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts that may be present or absent without being perceived are not organic parts of the whole; aim for interdependence among incidents and elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the poet as maker of plots
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet (maker) ought to be primarily a constructor of plots (imitator of actions) rather than merely an arranger of metres or versifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when taking historical material, the poet composes to express what is possible and universal; inventiveness and crafting of action is the poet's chief skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of names/subjects: plausibility over strict fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic subject-matter may use familiar or fictitious names; what matters is that the action be possible and credible, not that it strictly follows received legends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar subjects please only a few directly but can please all; poets need not bind themselves to traditional stories if invented plots maintain internal probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and diction should reflect the mode of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Meter and diction should fit the type of speech represented: iambic aligns with colloquial conversational speech; hexameter suits epic narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once dialogue arrives, Nature provides the appropriate measure (e.g., iambic for colloquial). Choose metrical forms that naturally echo the register of the characters and situations.
